questions.title: How does DPO optimize for human preferences without an explicit reward model?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the fundamental difference between RLHF and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). The paper states that DPO eliminates the need for explicit reward modeling and reinforcement learning. However, if there is no reward model being trained, what is the objective function actually 'rewarding' during the optimization process? Is it simply looking at the labels of the preferred completions, or is there still an underlying reward representation being updated?

questions.title: Why does the partition function $Z(x)$ cancel out in the derivation of the DPO objective?
questions.question_body: In Section 4, the paper derives the optimal policy $\pi_r(y|x)$ in Equation 5, which includes a partition function $Z(x)$. When they move to Equation 6, they claim that $Z(x)$ cancels out because the Bradley-Terry model depends only on the difference of rewards between two completions. Can someone explain the algebraic steps or the intuition behind why a term that depends on the prefix $x$ but not the completion $y$ disappears when we look at the difference $r^*(x, y_1) - r^*(x, y_2)$?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the 'dynamic, per-example importance weight' in the DPO gradient?
questions.question_body: In the analysis of the DPO gradient (Equation 10), the paper mentions a 'higher weight when reward estimate is wrong.' Specifically, the gradient is weighted by $\sigma(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w))$. I'm confused about how this weight functions. If the model already correctly predicts that the preferred completion $y_w$ has a higher reward than $y_l$, does the gradient become smaller? How does this specific weighting prevent the 'model degeneration' mentioned in the abstract?

questions.title: How does the equivalence relation between reward functions justify the DPO reparameterization?
questions.question_body: Section 5.1 introduces an equivalence relation where two rewards are equivalent if they differ only by a function of the prefix $f(x)$. The paper uses this to prove Theorem 1, which says DPO doesn't lose any generality. I'm struggling to understand the connection: why is it sufficient to only recover an 'arbitrary' reward function from the optimal class? If we are missing the specific $f(x)$ part of the reward, does that actually matter for the final policy $\pi_\theta$?

questions.title: How does initializing $\pi_{ref}$ via maximum likelihood mitigate distribution shift in DPO?
questions.question_body: In the DPO outline, the authors suggest that if $\pi^{SFT}$ is unavailable, $\pi_{ref}$ should be initialized by maximizing the likelihood of preferred completions $(x, y_w)$. The paper claims this helps 'mitigate the distribution shift.' Could someone explain why maximizing the likelihood of preferred completions is a better way to handle distribution shift than simply using a generic pre-trained language model as the reference?

questions.title: Does the $\beta$ parameter in DPO represent the same concept as the $\beta$ in the KL-constrained RL objective?
questions.question_body: In Equation 3, $\beta$ is the coefficient for the KL-divergence constraint. In the DPO objective (Equation 8), $\beta$ appears inside the log terms. Are these mathematically the same $\beta$? If I change $\beta$ in the DPO loss, is it behaving identically to how $\beta$ constrains the policy in the PPO-based RLHF pipeline, or does the change-of-variables introduce a different behavior?
